pos: n. (the power of speech given; rendering Greek apophtheggomai and logos)
etymology: From utter, to put forth. In the New Testament utterance is nearly always something given rather than achieved.
biblical_def: Utterance is granted speech. At Pentecost the disciples “began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance” (Act 2:4) — the words were theirs to say and His to give. Paul asks the Ephesians to pray “that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel” (Eph 6:19), and asks the Colossians for “a door of utterance, to speak the mystery of Christ” (Col 4:3). He commends the Corinthians for abounding in it (1Co 1:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines utterance as the act of uttering words; pronunciation; manner of speaking; and vocal expression.
webster_full: UTTERANCE, n. The act of uttering words; pronunciation; manner of speaking.
2. Vocal expression; as, to give utterance to one's feelings.
scriptures: Act 2:4
And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.
Eph 6:19
And for me, that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel,
Col 4:3
Withal praying also for us, that God would open unto us a door of utterance, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds:
That in every thing ye are enriched by him, in all utterance, and in all knowledge;
corruption_summary: Eloquence is trained and utterance is assumed, when the apostle who could out-argue anyone asked churches to pray he would be given words at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 6:19 is startling in context. Paul has just described the whole armour of God and then asks for prayer — for himself, the most capable communicator in the early church — that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly. He does not ask for opportunity alone, or courage alone, but for the words. A man who thought his fluency was his own would never make that request.

Colossians 4:3 shows what he wants the door opened for: withal praying also for us, that God would open unto us a door of utterance, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds. He was in prison when he wrote it. The door he asks for is not release but speech — which reorders what a suffering Christian might reasonably ask his friends to pray.
roots_summary: Greek apophtheggomai (G669), to speak out, declare; logos (G3056), a word or discourse — Paul's term when he asks for utterance to be given.
roots_lines: Greek apophtheggomai (G669) — to speak forth; Acts 2:4, 14, 26:25.
Greek logos (G3056) — word, utterance; Ephesians 6:19, Colossians 4:3, 1 Corinthians 1:5.
Greek parrhesia (G3954) — boldness, freedom of speech; the companion request in Ephesians 6:19-20.
usage: “As the Spirit gave them utterance” — theirs to say, His to give.
“That utterance may be given unto me” — Paul asking for words.
“A door of utterance” — what a prisoner asked prayer for instead of release.

etymology: From Latin communicare, to share. In the KJV communication means talk — what passes between people — not the modern discipline of messaging.
biblical_def: Communication is speech shared between people. Christ sets the plainest standard: “let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil” (Mat 5:37). Paul warns the Corinthians that “evil communications corrupt good manners” (1Co 15:33), and instructs the Ephesians, “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers” (Eph 4:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines communication as the act of imparting; intercourse by words, letters or messages; interchange of thoughts or opinions.
webster_full: COMMUNICATION, n. The act of imparting, conferring, or delivering, from one to another.
2. Intercourse by words, letters or messages; interchange of thoughts or opinions, by conference or other means.
3. Connection by means of a passage.
scriptures: Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Eph 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.
Col 4:6
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
corruption_summary: Speech is judged by whether it was technically true, when Paul's test is whether it built anyone up — a standard that condemns a great deal of accurate talk.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 4:29 sets a bar most Christian conversation fails. Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers. The positive standard is the demanding half: speech is meant to build, and to hand grace to the person listening. Gossip fails it, but so does much accurate criticism, much venting, and much talk that merely passes time without harming anyone.

Matthew 5:37 addresses the opposite problem — speech inflated to be believed. Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay. Christ is discussing oaths, and His reasoning is that elaborate assurance is a symptom: a man whose plain word is reliable has no need of it. Where every statement requires an intensifier, the currency has already been debased.
roots_summary: Greek logos (G3056), word, speech; homilia (G3657), association, converse — the word behind evil communications in 1 Corinthians 15:33.
roots_lines: Greek logos (G3056) — word, communication; Matthew 5:37, Ephesians 4:29.
Greek homilia (G3657) — company, converse; 1 Corinthians 15:33, evil communications corrupt good manners.
Greek oikodome (G3619) — building up, edifying; the stated purpose of Christian speech.
usage: “Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay” — plain speech needs no intensifier.
“That it may minister grace unto the hearers” — the demanding positive standard.
“Evil communications corrupt good manners” — company shapes character.

etymology: From Latin salutare, to wish health. A salutation is a wish for another's welfare, formalized into a greeting.
biblical_def: A salutation is a greeting. Elisabeth's response to Mary's makes it more than courtesy: “when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb” (Luk 1:41). Christ rebukes scribes who love “greetings in the markets” (Mar 12:38), and Paul signs letters with his own hand: “The salutation of me Paul with mine own hand, which is the token in every epistle” (2Th 3:17). John forbids greeting a false teacher who brings not the doctrine of Christ, “for he that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds” (2Jn 10–11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines salutation as the act of saluting; a greeting; the act of paying respect or reverence by the customary words or actions.
webster_full: SALUTATION, n. The act of saluting; a greeting; the act of paying respect or reverence by the customary words or actions.
2. Quotation of respect or kindness.
scriptures: Luk 1:41
And it came to pass, that, when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost:
And he said unto them in his doctrine, Beware of the scribes, which love to go in long clothing, and love salutations in the marketplaces,
The salutation of Paul with mine own hand, which is the token in every epistle: so I write.
2Jn 10
If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed:
corruption_summary: Greeting is treated as neutral politeness, but Scripture makes it a signal — which is why John forbids extending one to a man denying Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 John 10-11 is the passage most modern readers stumble over: if there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed: for he that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds. This is not about rudeness to strangers or refusing to converse with unbelievers; the subject is a travelling teacher denying that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh, and the hospitality in question would have endorsed and funded his mission. A greeting, in that setting, was a credential.

Luke 1:41 shows the other extreme — a salutation carrying real power. When Elisabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb, and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost. Two pregnant women exchange a greeting in the hill country of Judea, and the forerunner responds to the presence of the Christ before either child is born. Not every hello is small.
roots_summary: Greek aspasmos (G783), a greeting or embrace; aspazomai (G782), to greet — the verb of the long lists of names in Romans 16.
roots_lines: Greek aspasmos (G783) — salutation; Luke 1:29, 41, 44, Mark 12:38, 1 Corinthians 16:21.
Greek aspazomai (G782) — to greet, salute; Romans 16, twenty-one times over.
Greek chairo (G5463) — to rejoice, be glad; the root of the common Greek greeting, and John's God speed in 2 John 10.
usage: “When Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary” — not every greeting is small.
“Love salutations in the marketplaces” — the scribes' appetite for public deference.
“Neither bid him God speed” — a greeting as a credential.

pos: adj. (praising falsely for advantage; rendering Hebrew chalaq, smooth)
etymology: From Old French flater, to stroke. The Hebrew root means smooth — flattery is speech with the friction taken out.
biblical_def: Flattering speech praises falsely to gain advantage. Scripture treats it as a trap laid by the speaker for the hearer: “A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet” (Pro 29:5). The strange woman's characteristic weapon is “the flattery of her lips” (Pro 7:21). Paul denies using it in ministry: “neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness” (1Th 2:5). The psalmist prays against “flattering lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things” (Psa 12:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines flatter as to gratify by praise; to please by applause; to soothe by praise or obsequiousness; and to raise false hopes.
webster_full: FLATTER, v.t. To gratify by praise; to please by applause; to soothe.
2. To please; to gratify; as, to flatter one's vanity.
3. To praise falsely; to encourage by favorable notice.
4. To raise false hopes by representation not well founded.
scriptures: Pro 29:5
A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet.
For neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness:
Psa 12:3
The LORD shall cut off all flattering lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things:
Pro 7:21
With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him.
corruption_summary: Flattery has become the ordinary dialect of platform ministry — audiences told what they wish about themselves — and it is nearly invisible because it is enjoyable.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 29:5 identifies flattery's mechanism precisely: a man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet. The flattered man is not merely misinformed; he is being positioned. That is why flattery is so difficult to detect from the inside — it arrives as affirmation, and refusing it feels like false modesty. The test is not whether the praise is pleasant but whether the speaker gains by my believing it.

1 Thessalonians 2:5 shows Paul's own boundary, and he pairs it with money for a reason: neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness. Flattery and greed travel together, because telling people what they want to hear is the cheapest way to keep them giving. A ministry that never says anything its supporters dislike has not necessarily lied, but it has built an incentive structure that will eventually require it to.
roots_summary: Hebrew chalaq (H2505), to be smooth, to flatter; cheleq, smoothness — the same root behind smooth words; Greek kolakeia (G2850), flattery.
roots_lines: Hebrew chalaq (H2505) — to be smooth, divide, flatter; Proverbs 29:5, Psalm 5:9, they flatter with their tongue.
Hebrew chelqah (H2513) — smoothness, flattery; Proverbs 7:21, with her much fair speech she caused him to yield.
Greek kolakeia (G2850) — flattery; only 1 Thessalonians 2:5.
usage: “A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet” — praise as positioning.
“Neither… flattering words… nor a cloke of covetousness” — the two travel together.
“The LORD shall cut off all flattering lips” — the psalmist's prayer.

pos: v. (to abuse with words; rendering Greek loidoreo)
etymology: From Old French reviler, to hold cheap. To revile is to speak in a way that reduces a person's worth in the hearing of others.
biblical_def: To revile is to abuse verbally. Christ places it in the beatitudes as a blessing: “Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake” (Mat 5:11). Peter describes the Lord's own response: “who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” (1Pe 2:23). Paul lists revilers among those who shall not inherit the kingdom (1Co 6:10) and reports his own practice: “being reviled, we bless” (1Co 4:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revile as to reproach; to treat with opprobrious and contemptuous language.
webster_full: REVILE, v.t. To reproach; to treat with opprobrious and contemptuous language.
REVILER, n. One who reviles another; one who treats another with contemptuous language.
scriptures: Mat 5:11
Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:
And labour, working with our own hands: being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it:
Nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: Reviling is now a genre with an audience, and Christians participate on the grounds that the target deserves it — a defence Peter never offers for the sinless Man who declined to use it.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Peter 2:23 gives the pattern and the mechanism together. Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously. The restraint is not stoicism or a superior temperament. It works by transfer: He handed the case to a Judge who would rule correctly, which freed Him from having to win the exchange. Anyone who must secure the verdict himself will always answer back.

1 Corinthians 6:10 puts revilers in a list that shocks by its company — alongside idolaters, thieves, drunkards, and extortioners. The church has generally treated the tongue's sins as venial and the body's as mortal, and Paul does not sort them that way. Nor does he leave the reviler without hope; the same passage adds, and such were some of you: but ye are washed.
roots_summary: Greek loidoreo (G3058), to rail at, revile; loidoros (G3060), a reviler; oneidizo (G3679), to reproach, in Matthew 5:11.
roots_lines: Greek loidoreo (G3058) — to revile, rail; John 9:28, 1 Peter 2:23, 1 Corinthians 4:12.
Greek loidoros (G3060) — a reviler; 1 Corinthians 5:11 and 6:10.
Greek oneidizo (G3679) — to reproach, upbraid; Matthew 5:11, when men shall revile you.
usage: “Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you… for my sake” — the qualifier matters.
“When he was reviled, reviled not again” — the case handed to a Judge.
“Being reviled, we bless” — the apostolic reflex.

pos: n. (a message or commission; rendering Hebrew dabar)
etymology: Old English aerende, a message. An errand is a task carried on someone else's behalf — the messenger's own preferences are not in it.
biblical_def: An errand is a commission carried for another. Abraham's servant refuses to eat until he has stated his: “I will not eat, until I have told mine errand” (Gen 24:33) — and the whole chapter turns on a servant who will not be distracted from his master's business. Jehu asks Jonadab nothing about the errand's content but demands allegiance (2Ki 9:5, in context of the young prophet's errand). Judges records Ehud's “secret errand unto thee, O king” (Jdg 3:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines errand as a verbal message; a mandate; something to be told or done; and the business on which a person is sent.
webster_full: ERRAND, n. A verbal message; a mandate; something to be told or done; the business on which a person is sent.
2. Any special business to be transacted by a messenger.
scriptures: And there was set meat before him to eat: but he said, I will not eat, until I have told mine errand. And he said, Speak on.
Jdg 3:19
But he himself turned again from the quarries that were by Gilgal, and said, I have a secret errand unto thee, O king: who said, Keep silence. And all that stood by him went out from him.
And when he came, behold, the captains of the host were sitting; and he said, I have an errand to thee, O captain. And Jehu said, Unto which of all us? And he said, To thee, O captain.
And he said unto them, Hinder me not, seeing the LORD hath prospered my way; send me away that I may go to my master.
corruption_summary: Christian service drifts into self-expression, where Genesis 24 shows a servant so gripped by his master's errand that he will not even eat until it is discharged.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 24 is the longest chapter in Genesis and it is entirely about a servant on an errand. He prays specifically, he watches for the answer, he worships when it comes, and when hospitality is offered he says, I will not eat, until I have told mine errand. Later, when the family asks him to stay ten days, his reply is the same instinct: hinder me not, seeing the LORD hath prospered my way. The errand governs his appetite and his calendar.

The servant is never named in the chapter. He is called the servant throughout, and his entire recorded speech is about his master and his master's son. That anonymity is part of the portrait: a man completely absorbed in someone else's business, who ends the chapter by handing over the bride and disappearing from the narrative. It is difficult to read Genesis 24 without seeing a picture of the Spirit's work.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar (H1697), word, matter, business — the same noun for a spoken word and for the errand it constitutes.
roots_lines: Hebrew dabar (H1697) — word, matter, errand; Genesis 24:33, Judges 3:19, 2 Kings 9:5.
Hebrew ebed (H5650) — servant; the unnamed figure of Genesis 24.
Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to prosper; Genesis 24:56, the LORD hath prospered my way.
usage: “I will not eat, until I have told mine errand” — the commission governs the appetite.
“Hinder me not, seeing the LORD hath prospered my way” — and the calendar.
“I have a secret errand unto thee, O king” — Ehud before Eglon.

pos: n. (an expressed grievance; rendering Hebrew siach and siyach)
etymology: From Latin complangere, to lament. Scripture distinguishes complaint addressed to God, which it records approvingly, from murmuring about Him, which it condemns.
biblical_def: A complaint is a grievance expressed. Job insists on his right to state one: “I will leave my complaint upon myself; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul” (Job 10:1). Hannah explains her silent lips to Eli: “out of the abundance of my complaint and grief have I spoken hitherto” (1Sa 1:16). David makes it a pattern of prayer: “I poured out my complaint before him; I shewed before him my trouble” (Psa 142:2). Acts records the Grecians' complaint about neglected widows, and the church acts on it (Act 6:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines complaint as expression of grief, regret, pain, censure or resentment; lamentation; and a representation of injuries.
webster_full: COMPLAINT, n. Expression of grief, regret, pain, censure, or resentment; lamentation; murmuring; a finding fault.
2. The cause or subject of complaint or murmuring.
3. A malady; a disease; usually applied to disorders not violent.
scriptures: Job 10:1
My soul is weary of my life; I will leave my complaint upon myself; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul.
Count not thine handmaid for a daughter of Belial: for out of the abundance of my complaint and grief have I spoken hitherto.
I poured out my complaint before him; I shewed before him my trouble.
Act 6:1
And in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration.
corruption_summary: Believers are taught that all complaint is unbelief, which drives real grief underground — when Scripture's own prayers are full of complaints addressed to the right Person.
corruption_paragraphs: The distinction Scripture maintains is not between complaining and not complaining but between complaining about God and complaining to Him. Israel murmured against Moses in the hearing of one another; David poured out his complaint before Him and shewed before Him his trouble. The same raw material — grievance, pain, confusion — is sin when circulated among the discontented and prayer when carried to the throne.

Acts 6:1 adds an institutional lesson the church regularly ignores. There arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration. The complaint was justified, and the apostles neither dismissed it nor absorbed it into their own work; they had the congregation appoint seven men to fix it. Some complaints are best answered by structural change rather than by exhortation to patience.
roots_summary: Hebrew siyach (H7879), meditation, complaint; siach (H7878), to muse or pour out speech; Greek goggusmos (G1112), murmuring, in Acts 6:1.
roots_lines: Hebrew siyach (H7879) — complaint, meditation; Job 10:1, 1 Samuel 1:16, Psalm 142:2.
Hebrew shaphak (H8210) — to pour out; Psalm 142:2, I poured out my complaint before him.
Greek goggusmos (G1112) — murmuring, complaint; Acts 6:1, a justified one.
usage: “I poured out my complaint before him” — addressed to the right Person.
“Out of the abundance of my complaint and grief have I spoken” — Hannah to Eli.
“Their widows were neglected” — a complaint answered by structure.

pos: n. (a dispute, a legal case; rendering Hebrew rib)
etymology: From Latin controversus, turned against. The Hebrew rib is a lawsuit — God's controversies are formal charges, not moods.
biblical_def: A controversy is a dispute, often a legal case. The prophets use it of God's suit against His people: “the LORD hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land, because there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God in the land” (Hos 4:1); “the LORD hath a controversy with his people, and he will plead with Israel” (Mic 6:2). The law assigns judges to settle human ones (Deu 17:8), and Paul names the greatest agreed truth as beyond dispute: “without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh” (1Ti 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines controversy as a dispute or debate; agitation of contrary opinions; and a suit in law, a case in court.
webster_full: CONTROVERSY, n. Dispute; debate; agitation of contrary opinions.
2. A suit in law; a case in which opposing parties contend for their respective claims before a tribunal.
3. Opposition; resistance.
scriptures: Hos 4:1
Hear the word of the LORD, ye children of Israel: for the LORD hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land, because there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God in the land.
Mic 6:2
Hear ye, O mountains, the LORD'S controversy, and ye strong foundations of the earth: for the LORD hath a controversy with his people, and he will plead with Israel.
Deu 17:8

If there arise a matter too hard for thee in judgment, between blood and blood, between plea and plea, and between stroke and stroke, being matters of controversy within thy gates: then shalt thou arise, and get thee up into the place which the LORD thy God shall choose;

And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.
corruption_summary: Doctrinal dispute is treated as inherently unspiritual, and everything is called a controversy — while Paul reserves without controversy for what the church actually holds in common.
corruption_paragraphs: Micah 6 stages God's controversy as a courtroom scene with the mountains summoned as witnesses, and the striking feature is the tone of the divine complaint: O my people, what have I done unto thee? and wherein have I wearied thee? testify against me. The Judge invites the defendant to state a grievance first. That is not weakness; it is the confidence of a plaintiff whose case is complete, and it gives the passage a tenderness that a bare indictment would lack.

1 Timothy 3:16 shows the other use of the word and the church's needed instinct. Without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory. There are matters genuinely in dispute and matters that are not, and a church that cannot tell the difference will either fight over everything or concede everything.
roots_summary: Hebrew rib (H7379), a lawsuit, contention; the verb rib means to plead a case; Greek homologoumenos (G3672), confessedly, without controversy.
roots_lines: Hebrew rib (H7379) — controversy, lawsuit; Hosea 4:1, Micah 6:2, Deuteronomy 17:8.
Hebrew yakach (H3198) — to reason, plead, reprove; Isaiah 1:18, let us reason together.
Greek homologoumenos (G3672) — confessedly, beyond dispute; only 1 Timothy 3:16.
usage: “The LORD hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land” — a formal charge.
“O my people, what have I done unto thee?” — the plaintiff invites the defence first.
“Without controversy great is the mystery of godliness” — what is not in dispute.
